stem: A client with diabetes has shortened red blood cell survival, making hemoglobin A1C difficult to interpret. The provider orders serum fructosamine to assess recent glycemic control. Which interpretation should the nurse use?

options.A: Fructosamine reflects intermediate glycemic control over roughly the previous 1 to 3 weeks and can be useful when red blood cell survival makes A1C unreliable.
options.B: Fructosamine reflects only the glucose concentration at the moment the blood sample is collected.
options.C: Fructosamine reflects approximately the same red-cell-based glycemic interval as A1C and is affected by red blood cell survival in the same way.
options.D: Fructosamine is primarily a six-month measure of glycemia and is therefore less responsive to recent changes than A1C.

rationale: A is correct. Mayo Clinic Laboratories describes serum fructosamine as a measure of intermediate glycemic control over approximately the previous 1 to 3 weeks and identifies it as useful for monitoring people with shortened red blood cell survival, when A1C may be misleading. Fructosamine measures glycated serum proteins, largely glycated albumin, rather than glycated hemoglobin. B confuses fructosamine with a point-in-time glucose measurement. C incorrectly treats fructosamine as red-cell dependent. D reverses its clinical time window.
educational_objective: Interpret serum fructosamine as an intermediate-term glycemic marker covering roughly 1 to 3 weeks and recognize its usefulness when altered red blood cell survival limits A1C interpretation.
source_version_date: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories test catalog accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: FRUCT — Useful For: monitoring intermediate 1–3 week glycemic control and patients with shortened red blood cell survival; Clinical Information/Interpretation: fructosamine measures glycated serum proteins and generally reflects the previous 1–3 weeks. Hemoglobin A1c, Blood — Cautions: shortened erythrocyte survival can produce misleading A1C and fructosamine may be used as an alternate measure
source_claim_supported: Serum fructosamine reflects intermediate glycemic control over approximately 1–3 weeks and can be useful when shortened red blood cell survival makes A1C unreliable.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential; interpret diagnostic laboratory studies and recognize factors that can alter test reliability
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — fructosamine interpretation when A1C is unreliable
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item to use Mayo’s directly supported 1–3 week interval rather than the narrower 2–3 week claim and replaced the broad ‘certain hemoglobin variants’ example with shortened red blood cell survival, a directly supported circumstance in which A1C interpretation is unreliable and fructosamine is useful.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified directly against current Mayo Clinic Laboratories FRUCT and A1C test information. Mayo gives a 1–3 week interval and explicitly identifies shortened RBC survival as a use case.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A uses the exact laboratory-supported time window and mechanism. The rationale distinguishes glycated serum proteins from glycated hemoglobin without asserting that fructosamine is free of all possible confounders.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; it matches both the timeframe and the clinically supported reason for choosing fructosamine.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; fructosamine is not a single-moment glucose test.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; fructosamine is serum-protein based rather than dependent on erythrocyte lifespan in the same way as A1C.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; its interval is shorter, not longer, than A1C.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A matches both the test biology and the current laboratory interpretation.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices are interpretations of the same laboratory test and timeframe.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential is appropriate because the nurse is interpreting a diagnostic marker selected because another test is unreliable.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked 1–3 versus 2–3 week precision, A1C/RBC-survival confounding, hemoglobin-variant overgeneralization, serum-protein mechanism, lab-source authority, and second-answer risk. No unresolved conflict remained.
